t.2.91.1: Then Rāma, having soothed Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, who was greatly agitated and overcome with anger, spoke these words.
t.2.91.2: What need is there here for a bow, or for a sword with a shield, when Bharata himself, the great archer of great wisdom, has come?
t.2.91.3: It is only fitting that Bharata here wishes to see us; he would not do anything harmful to us, not even in his mind.
t.2.91.4: When, and what, wrong has Bharata ever done to you before? Or what fear such as this do you have today, that you suspect Bharata here?
t.2.91.5: Bharata must not be addressed by you with harsh words, nor with unkind speech; for if anything unkind is done to Bharata, it is I who would have been spoken to unkindly.
t.2.91.6: How indeed could sons slay their father, in whatever calamity, or a brother slay his brother, O Saumitri, who is his own very life-breath?
t.2.91.7: If you speak these words for the sake of the kingdom, then on seeing Bharata I shall tell him, "Let the kingdom be given to this one."
t.2.91.8: For indeed, Lakṣmaṇa, if Bharata is told by me in earnest, 'Give the kingdom to him,' he will say nothing but 'Certainly!'
t.2.91.9: Thus addressed by his righteous brother, Lakṣmaṇa, ever devoted to his welfare, seemed to shrink into his own limbs out of shame.
t.2.91.10: Seeing Lakṣmaṇa abashed, Rāghava replied: "This mighty-armed one, I think, has come here to see us."
t.2.91.11: Having reflected on the life of dwelling in the forest, he will lead them back home, or at least this Vaidehī, who has always been accustomed to the utmost comfort.
t.2.91.13: That very elephant of huge body, swaying at the head of the army, is the elephant named Śatruṃjaya, the aged mount of my wise father.
t.2.91.12: Here those two excellent horses come into full view, O hero, charming, of noble breed, swift and equal to the wind in speed.
t.2.91.14: Having climbed down from the top of that sāla tree, Lakṣmaṇa, victorious in battle, stood beside Rāma with his palms joined in reverence.
t.2.91.15: Then, instructed by Bharata that there should be no crowding, the army set up its encampment all around that mountain.
t.2.91.16: That army of the Ikṣvākus, crowded with elephants, horses and chariots, encamped on the flank of the mountain, covering an area of a yojana and a half.
t.2.91.17: That army, led to Citrakūṭa by the prudent Bharata, who had placed dharma foremost and cast off pride in order to win the favour of Raghunandana, shines forth resplendent.
